text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

White sugar futures in London remained subdued with most contracts ending in the minus column. August closed up 70 cents at $313.0 per tonne, while October lost 70 cents to close at $303.0 per tonne. Raw sugar futures in New York settled mixed. July added 4 points to close at 10.88 cents/lb, while October closed 1 point higher at 10.70 cents/lb. The outer months lost between 1 and 3 points. There was no fresh news to influence prices. The International Sugar Organization in London (ISO) made a new assessment of supply and demand 1996/97 with the production figure for 1996/97 only slightly below our estimate released in February. However, the consumption estimate is somewhat above our February prediction.

ISO - World sugar production should reach 123.49 mn tonnes, raw value, in 1996/97 (October/September), down on the 124.19 mn tonnes produced the previous year. Consumption in 1996/97 is estimated at 121.20 mn tonnes, 2.1 per cent above the 1995/96 figure of 118.656 tonnes. The 1996/97 sugar surplus is expected to be sharply lower at 2.29 mn tonnes, compared with 5.54 mn tonnes the previous year, the ISO said.

It was emphasized that world production in the current crop cycle will be 0.708 mn tonnes short from the record 124.193 mn tonnes achieved in the previous crop year but 8.123 mn tonnes up compared to 1994/95. The ISO said for the time being world export availability is expected to exceed import demand by 1.88 mn tonnes in 1996/97.

If the trade estimate remains valid until the end of the cycle, exportable but unsold sugars will be added to the new season's beginning stocks. This pessimistic but realistic scenario will make the stocks at the beginning of the forthcoming 1997/98 crop cycle as high as 42.8 mn tonnes, or 35 per cent of this crop year's world consumption, the ISO said.

It was added: 'we continue to expect that the downward pressure of the bearish global fundamentals has not yet been exhausted and, at least, the upward potential of the market inspired by some events with a bullish interpretation (e.g., the cyclone Justin's damage to the Australian crop, a further reduction of Indian production or recent buying activities of Russia, etc.) is limited.

However, the actual surplus in 1996/97 may be lower than indicated by the ISO for the following two reasons: a) the surplus figure of 2.29 mn tonnes does not take account of unrecorded disappearance and b) the ISO production estimate seems to be fairly generous.

THAILAND - Thailand's 1996/97 season (November/October) has drawn to a close with the country's 46 mills reported to have closed for the season. The Thai Cane and Sugar Corporation has pegged the national output at 5.8 million tonnes, tel quel, down from the previous year's production of 6.03 million tonnes. The decline is attributed to labour shortages and flooding.

BRAZIL - Sugar output in the 1996/97 campaign (May/April) up to April 16, 1997 amounted to 13.606 mn tonnes, tel quel, of which 10.421 mn tonnes in the Center-South and 3.185 mn tonnes in the North/Northeast. The crop plan for 1996/97 calls for an overall production of 14.446 mn tonnes, of which 10.974 mn tonnes in the Center-South and 3.471 mn tonnes in the North/Northeast. Comparable figures for the previous year are not available as the campaign 1996/97 already started in April instead of May. In the meantime it is being reported that the cane belt in the states of Sao Paulo and Parana continues to be dry with no rainfall in some areas for over 30 days. According to industry sources, rains are needed for the cane to complete its development phase. However, the recent dry conditions have proved to be favourable for an early harvest.

Tunisia bought a cargo of 14,000 tonnes of raw sugar at $276.90 per tonne c&f. Further details were not immediately available. State-owned Taiwan Sugar Corporation recently bought 30,000 tonnes of Australian raw sugar at a tender in New York city for June 5-20 arrival in Taiwan. Company officials declined to disclose purchase prices. The state-run Trading Corporation of Pakistan (TCP) invited bids, to be opened on May 24, for 50,000 tonnes of white refined crystal sugar to be delivered in two equal shipments by June 30 and July 15.
